gib_airfield.text: RAF Gibraltar Movements. Say the word and the Airbridge takes you home to Brize Norton.

gib_cop.text: Mind the runway, please. If you hear the siren, stop. If you see a plane, definitely stop.
Gibraltar has one of the smallest police forces anywhere, and one of the biggest views from the beat.

gib_llanito.text: We speak Llanito here: English and Spanish tangled up together, with a bit of Genoese and Maltese for flavour. 'Yaniti' is the Llanito for what you'd call a bit of a mess, and 'mira' is how you get everyone's attention.
The old rule is you can start a sentence in English and end it in Spanish, and it'll still be correct somewhere.

gib_calentita.text: Calentita is our national dish: a baked cake of chickpea flour, olive oil, water, salt and pepper, hot from the oven. The name is just 'little hot one' in Spanish. The Genoese brought it with them from Liguria, where they call it farinata.
Eat it with black pepper, and a splash of lemon if you've got a taste for such things.

gib_regiment.text: The Royal Gibraltar Regiment is the Rock's own regiment, and its soldiers are mostly local. The regiment's badge has the castle and key of Gibraltar.
The castle and key was granted in 1502 by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and the Rock still uses it today.

gib_fisher.text: The Bay's full of bream and mullet, and a few things I'd rather not catch. The dolphins are a nuisance and a joy; they take my bait and then wave.
My granddad fished here before the border closed in 1969. Fifteen years of seeing Spain across the water, and nobody could cross.

gib_dolphin_watcher.text: Dolphin trip, two hours, guaranteed dolphins or you can have your money back. Well, you'll see the sea. And probably dolphins.
We go out past the Bay to the Strait. On a clear day you can see Morocco, with Jebel Musa on the African side, the other Pillar of Hercules.

gib_pilot.text: Landing here is the aviation equivalent of parking in a tight bay with a very big audience. The Rock throws up a curl of wind that can slap you sideways, called the Levanter.
When the Levanter blows, a cloud sits over the Rock like a flat white tablecloth. It isn't an omen. It's just the wind meeting a mountain.

gib_gardener.text: The Alameda Gardens are the Rock's botanical gardens, laid out in the early 1800s by the Governor. The wishing well is still there, if you've a spare coin.
A lot of what grows here is from the Mediterranean and Africa. The Governor of the day had a taste for exotic plants, and the soil agreed with them.

gib_guard.text: I'm a ceremonial guard, but don't be fooled. If you start taking photos while I'm marching, I'll be a very polite guard indeed, with a very large rifle.
The Changing of the Guard is at the Convent a few days a week. Come on a Tuesday in summer; it's the best seat in the house.

gib_scholar.text: I'm writing a dissertation on the Great Siege. There were more guns on this Rock than there were people in some English towns.
The Garrison Library has the siege accounts of Captain John Drinkwater, who was there. His book is the best account of the siege in English.

gibraltar_bureau.text: Gibraltar pounds are at par with sterling, and every shop here takes your English money one for one. Mind, the Rock only hands out its own notes, and the mainland won't take them back.
